title: The Brave Little Camel
summary: A young camel struggling to keep up on her first desert journey senses an approaching sandstorm before the herders do, and earns their respect.
poll: A small or inexperienced member of a group cannot really help the group in a dangerous moment.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Amal is a young camel. This is her first trip. She walks with a caravan. A caravan is camels and people. They cross the desert.

Amal is small. She is not fast. She falls behind a lot. An old herder named Jaber shakes his head. He does not think she can go all the way.

One day, the air goes still. Amal stops. She lifts her nose. She sniffs the air. Something is wrong. She will not move. She pulls back.

Jaber tells her to walk. Amal will not go. She groans. She pushes on her mom. The herders look up. Sand is rising far off. A big sandstorm comes!

The herders run to the rocks. They hide by a big dune. The storm goes past them.

After the storm, Jaber pats Amal. She felt it first. Now they feed her first. Amal is small. But she is brave.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Amal is a young camel. This is her first big trip. She walks with a caravan. A caravan is a group of camels and people. They are crossing the desert together.

Amal is still small. She is not as fast as the big camels. She falls behind again and again. An old herder named Jaber shakes his head at her. He does not think she can make it all the way.

One day, the air goes very still. Amal stops walking. She lifts her nose and sniffs. Something feels wrong to her. She will not move. She pulls back hard.

Jaber tells her to walk on. Amal still will not go. She groans and pushes on her mom. The herders stop and look up. Sand is rising fast, far off. A big sandstorm is coming their way!

The herders run to find rocks. They hide behind a tall dune just in time. The storm roars past them all.

After the storm, Jaber walks over and pats Amal. She felt the storm coming first. Now the herders feed her first each day. Amal is still small. But now she is the brave one too.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Picture a long line of camels moving across golden sand. This caravan is crossing the desert. Among the camels walks Amal, a young camel on her first long trip.

Amal is still small. She cannot walk as fast as the older camels. She falls behind again and again. A herder named Jaber shakes his head at her. He does not think she has the strength to finish the trip.

One hot day, something strange happens. The air grows very still. Even the wind seems to stop. Amal stops walking right where she stands. She lifts her nose and sniffs the air. Something feels wrong, but she cannot say why. She will not move forward, no matter what anyone tries.

Jaber tells her firmly to keep walking. Amal still will not take a step. She groans and pushes her body against her mother. The herders stop and look up at the sky. Far off, a wall of dark sand is rising fast. A big sandstorm is coming toward them!

The herders run to find rocks nearby. They hide behind a tall dune just in time. The storm blows past them with great force.

After the storm passes, Jaber walks over and pats Amal. She had felt the storm coming before any human saw a sign of it. From that day on, the herders feed her first each morning. Amal is no longer the smallest, weakest camel. She is the bravest one of all.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Picture a long line of camels moving across golden sand. This caravan is crossing the desert on a trip that will take many days. Walking near the middle is Amal, a young camel on her first long journey.

Amal is still small compared to the others. She cannot keep up with the older, stronger camels. She falls behind again and again. A herder named Jaber shakes his head every time he looks back at her. He does not believe the small camel has the strength to finish such a hard trip.

One hot afternoon, something strange happens. The air grows completely still. Even the desert wind seems to vanish. Amal stops walking right where she stands. She lifts her nose high and sniffs, again and again. Something feels deeply wrong. She will not move forward, no matter how hard anyone pulls.

Jaber orders her firmly to keep moving. Amal still will not take another step. She groans loudly and pushes her body against her mother's side. Confused, the herders finally pause and look up at the sky. Far off, a tall wall of dark sand is rising fast. A big sandstorm is racing toward the caravan!

The herders scramble to find rocks nearby. They crowd behind a tall, steep dune just in time. The storm roars past them with great force, shaking the ground.

After the storm passes, Jaber walks over and pats Amal with real thanks in his eyes. She had sensed the danger long before any human saw a single warning sign. From that day on, the herders feed her first every morning. Amal is no longer the smallest, weakest camel in the caravan. She has become, in everyone's eyes, the bravest one of all.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Picture a long line of camels walking across golden sand. Each one carries supplies for a trip that will take many days. This caravan is crossing the desert. Walking near the back, trying hard to keep up, is Amal, a young camel on her first long trip.

Amal is still much smaller than the camels around her. She cannot match their pace. She falls behind again and again, growing more exhausted with every hour. A herder named Jaber shakes his head at her. He doubts that such a small, stubborn animal has the strength to finish this trip.

One hot day, something strange happens. The air grows still, and even the wind seems to stop. Amal stops walking, every muscle tense. Some old instinct tells her that danger is near, long before her eyes can see it. She sniffs the air again and again, then will not take another step.

Jaber tells her firmly to keep moving, but Amal stays stubborn. She groans loudly and presses her body against her mother's side. Confused, the herders stop and look up at the sky. Far off, a tall wall of dark sand is rising fast. A big sandstorm is racing toward them!

The herders run to find shelter among nearby rocks. They crowd behind a tall dune just as the storm hits. It roars past them with great force, but everyone stays safe.

After the storm, Jaber walks over and pats Amal with real respect. Her strange instinct had warned them of the danger long before any human saw a sign of it. From that day on, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel differently, feeding her first. Loyal, clever Amal is no longer seen as the weakest camel in the caravan. She has proven, through one afternoon, that she is among the bravest.

A herder named Jaber shakes his head at her. Privately, he doubts that such a small, stubborn animal has the strength to finish this hard trip.

One hot afternoon, something strange happens. The air grows completely still, and even the wind seems to vanish. Amal stops walking, every muscle tense and alert. Some old instinct, passed down by many camels before her, tells her that danger is near long before her eyes can see it. She sniffs the heavy air again and again, then plants her feet and will not take another step.

Jaber orders her to keep moving, but Amal stays completely stubborn, pushing her weight back instead. She groans loudly and pushes her body against her mother's side, as if trying to warn her too. Confused, the herders finally pause and look up at the sky. Far off, a tall wall of dark sand is rising fast and racing toward them.

The herders rush to find shelter among nearby rocks, crowding behind a tall, steep dune just as the storm hits. It roars past them with great force, shaking the ground, but everyone stays safe.

After the storm, Jaber walks over slowly and pats Amal with real respect in his tired eyes. Her strange, stubborn instinct had warned the caravan of the danger long before any human saw a sign of it. From that day on, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel differently, feeding her first each morning. Loyal, clever Amal is no longer seen as the weakest camel in the caravan. She has proven, through one remarkable afternoon, that even the smallest among them can be the bravest of all.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Picture a long line of camels walking across golden sand. Every one carries supplies for a trading trip that will take many days between desert oases. This caravan is crossing the desert. Walking near the back, trying hard to keep up with the rest, is Amal, a young camel on her first long trip away from home.

Amal is still much smaller than the camels around her. She cannot match their steady pace across the shifting sand. She falls behind again and again, growing more exhausted with every hour of the hot afternoon. A herder named Jaber, who has led caravans across this desert for twenty years, shakes his head at her. Privately, he doubts that such a small, stubborn animal has the strength or endurance to survive this hard trip.

One hot afternoon, something strange happens that catches the caravan by surprise. The air suddenly grows still, and even the wind seems to vanish without warning. Amal stops walking, every muscle tense and alert. Some old instinct, passed down by many camels before her, tells her that danger is gathering near, long before her eyes could see even a sign of it. She sniffs the heavy air again and again, then plants her feet and refuses to take another step, no matter how hard anyone pulls her rope.

Jaber orders her to keep moving, but Amal stays completely stubborn, pushing her weight back with surprising strength. She groans loudly and pushes her body against her mother's side, as if trying to warn her too. Confused and frustrated, the herders finally pause and look up at the darkening sky. Far off, a tall wall of dark sand is rising fast and racing straight toward the caravan.

The herders rush to find shelter among nearby rocks, crowding behind a tall, steep dune just as the storm hits. It roars past them with great force, shaking the ground, yet everyone stays safe inside their shelter.

After the storm passes and calm returns to the desert, Jaber walks over slowly and pats Amal with real respect shining in his tired eyes. Her strange, stubborn instinct had warned the caravan of the danger long before any human saw a sign of trouble. From that day on, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel differently, feeding her first each morning and watching her with quiet admiration. Loyal, clever Amal is no longer seen as the weakest camel in the caravan, but rather as proof that respect must sometimes be earned through surprise. She has shown, through one remarkable afternoon, that even the smallest and youngest among them can become the bravest of all.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Across a wide, rolling sea of golden sand, a caravan of Bedouin herders and their camels makes its way slowly toward a distant oasis, each animal carrying supplies for a trip that will last many days. Walking near the back, trying hard to match the steady pace of the group, is Amal, a young camel on her first long trip away from home.

Amal is still much smaller than the grown camels around her, and she lacks their practiced endurance across such shifting ground. She falls behind again and again, growing more tired with every hour under the harsh sun. Jaber, a Bedouin herder who has guided caravans across this desert for more than two decades, shakes his head whenever he glances back to gauge her progress. Privately, he doubts that such a small, stubborn young animal has enough strength or endurance to survive a trip this hard.

One hot afternoon, something strange happens that catches the whole caravan by surprise. The air suddenly grows unnaturally still, and even the steady desert wind seems to vanish without warning. Amal stops in her tracks, every muscle tense and alert to something unseen. An old instinct, carried by generations of desert camels, tells her that danger is gathering near, long before any human eye could notice a single sign of it. She sniffs the heavy air again and again, then plants her feet firmly, refusing to take another step no matter how hard anyone tugs at her rope.

Jaber orders her sharply to keep moving, yet Amal stays utterly stubborn, pulling backward with surprising strength. She groans loudly and presses her whole body against her mother's side, as though trying to warn her too. Baffled by this strange behavior, the herders finally pause and look up toward the darkening sky. Far off on the horizon, a huge wall of dark, swirling sand is rising fast, racing straight toward the exposed caravan.

The herders scramble at once to find shelter among nearby rocks, crowding behind a tall, steep dune just as the storm's first gusts arrive. The sandstorm thunders past them with great force, shaking the ground, yet everyone survives unharmed in their shelter.

After the storm finally passes and calm settles over the desert, Jaber walks over slowly and pats Amal with real, honest respect in his tired eyes. Her strange, stubborn instinct had warned the caravan of danger long before any human noticed even a single sign of trouble. From that day on, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel quite differently, feeding her first each morning and relying on her instincts whenever the weather feels uncertain. Loyal, clever Amal is no longer seen as the weakest camel in the caravan, but rather as proof that real respect must sometimes be earned through unexpected, admirable moments of courage. She has shown, through one remarkable afternoon, that even the smallest and youngest among a group can prove the bravest of all.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Across a wide, rolling sea of golden sand, a caravan of Bedouin herders and their camels makes its way slowly toward a distant oasis, each animal carrying supplies for a trading trip that will last many days across difficult ground. Walking near the back, trying hard to match the steady pace of the group, is Amal, a young camel on her first long trip away from the safety of home.

Amal is still much smaller than the grown camels moving confidently around her, and she lacks their practiced endurance across such punishing, shifting ground. She falls behind again and again, growing more tired with every hour under the harsh, relentless sun. Jaber, a Bedouin herder who has guided caravans across this desert for more than two decades, shakes his head skeptically each time he glances back to gauge her slowing progress. Privately, he doubts that such a small, stubborn young animal has enough strength or endurance to survive a trip this physically demanding.

One scorching afternoon, something strange happens that catches the whole caravan completely by surprise. The air suddenly grows unnaturally still, and even the steady desert wind seems to vanish without the slightest warning. Amal stops in her tracks, every muscle tense and alert to some unseen presence. An old instinct, carried silently by generations of desert camels, tells her that danger is gathering near, long before any human eye could notice a single sign of it. She sniffs the heavy, strange air again and again, then plants her feet firmly, refusing to take another step no matter how hard anyone tugs at her lead rope.

Jaber orders her sharply to keep moving, yet Amal stays utterly stubborn, pulling backward with surprising strength for such a small animal. She groans loudly and presses her whole body against her mother's side, as though trying desperately to warn her too. Baffled and frustrated by this strange behavior, the herders finally pause and look up toward the rapidly darkening sky. Far off on the horizon, a huge wall of dark, swirling sand is rising fast, racing straight toward the exposed, vulnerable caravan.

The herders scramble at once to find shelter among nearby rocky outcrops, crowding behind a tall, steep dune just as the storm's first violent gusts arrive. The sandstorm thunders past them with great, overwhelming force, shaking the very ground, yet everyone survives unharmed in their shelter.

After the storm finally passes and calm settles once more over the desert, Jaber walks over slowly and pats Amal with real, honest respect shining in his tired, weathered eyes. Her strange, stubborn instinct had warned the caravan of danger long before any human had noticed even a single sign of trouble. He realizes, perhaps for the first time, that generations of Bedouin wisdom have always held that the youngest animals sometimes sense what experience alone cannot teach. From that day on, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel quite differently, feeding her first each morning and relying on her instincts whenever the weather feels uncertain or threatening. Loyal, clever Amal is no longer seen as the weakest camel in the caravan, but rather as proof that real respect must sometimes be earned through unexpected, admirable moments of courage. She has shown, through one remarkable and frightening afternoon, that even the smallest and youngest among a group can prove the bravest of all.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Across a wide, rolling sea of golden sand, a caravan of Bedouin herders and their camels makes its way slowly toward a distant oasis, each animal carrying supplies for a trading expedition that will last many demanding days across difficult ground. Walking near the back, struggling constantly to match the steady pace of the group, is Amal, a young camel on her first long journey away from the safety of home.

Amal is still considerably smaller than the seasoned camels moving confidently around her, and she lacks their practiced endurance across such punishing, constantly shifting ground. She falls behind again and again, growing more fatigued with every hour under the harsh, relentless sun. Jaber, a Bedouin herder who has guided caravans across this desert for more than two decades, shakes his head skeptically each time he glances back to gauge her slowing progress. Privately, he doubts that such a small, obstinate young animal has sufficient strength or endurance to survive a journey this physically demanding.

One scorching afternoon, something peculiar happens that catches the whole caravan completely by surprise. The air suddenly grows unnaturally still, and even the steady desert wind seems to vanish without the slightest warning. Amal halts abruptly in her tracks, every muscle tensed and alert to some unseen, approaching presence. An ancient instinct, carried silently through generations of desert camels, tells her that danger is gathering nearby, long before any human eye could possibly notice a single visible sign of it. She sniffs the heavy, strangely charged air again and again, then plants her feet firmly, refusing to take another step no matter how insistently anyone tugs at her lead rope.

Jaber commands her sharply to keep moving, yet Amal remains utterly obstinate, pulling backward with surprising strength for such a small animal. She groans loudly and presses her whole body against her mother's side, as though trying desperately to warn her too. Baffled and growing frustrated by this strange behavior, the herders finally pause and gaze upward toward the rapidly darkening sky. Far off on the horizon, an enormous wall of dark, swirling sand is rising rapidly, racing directly toward the exposed, vulnerable caravan.

The herders scramble at once to locate shelter among nearby rocky outcrops, huddling behind a tall, steep dune just as the storm's first violent gusts strike. The sandstorm thunders past them with overwhelming force, shaking the very ground, yet everyone survives unharmed within their shelter.

For many years, desert travelers have noticed that camels often grow restless, or even stubbornly refuse to move, just before a sandstorm arrives, as though some shift in the air warns them long before any human instrument could gauge the coming danger.

After the storm finally subsides and calm settles once more over the desert, Jaber approaches slowly and pats Amal with unmistakable, honest respect shining in his weathered eyes. Her peculiar, stubborn instinct had warned the caravan of approaching danger long before any human had managed to notice even a single sign of trouble. He realizes, perhaps for the first time in many years, that generations of Bedouin wisdom have always held that even the youngest animals sometimes sense what human experience alone cannot teach. From that day forward, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel quite differently, feeding her first each morning and relying on her instincts whenever the weather seems uncertain or threatening. Loyal, perceptive Amal is no longer regarded as the weakest camel in the caravan, but rather as proof that genuine respect must sometimes be earned through unexpected, admirable moments of courage.

versions.title: The Brave Little Camel
versions.text:
Across a vast, undulating sea of golden sand, a caravan of Bedouin herders and their camels makes its way slowly toward a distant oasis, each heavily laden animal transporting goods for a trading expedition that will last many arduous days across difficult, unpredictable terrain. Somewhere near the rear of this slow-moving procession, struggling constantly to match the steady rhythm established by the group, walks Amal, a young camel experiencing her very first extended journey away from the safety and familiarity of home.

Amal remains considerably smaller than the seasoned adult camels moving confidently around her, and she simply lacks their practiced endurance across such punishing, constantly shifting terrain. She falls behind again and again, growing more fatigued with every grueling hour beneath the relentless desert sun. Jaber, an experienced Bedouin herder who has guided caravans across this unforgiving landscape for more than two decades, shakes his head skeptically each time he glances backward to gauge her steadily slowing progress. Privately, he doubts that such a small, obstinate young animal possesses sufficient strength or endurance to survive a journey this physically demanding.

One scorching afternoon, something peculiar happens that catches the entire caravan completely by surprise. The air suddenly grows unnaturally, almost eerily still, and even the ever-present desert wind seems to vanish entirely without the slightest warning sign. Amal halts abruptly in her tracks, every muscle in her compact frame tensed and alert to some unseen, approaching presence. An ancient instinct, inherited silently through countless generations of desert-born camels, tells her that danger is gathering nearby long before human eyes or ears could possibly detect even a single visible sign of it. She lifts her nose and sniffs repeatedly at the heavy, strangely charged air, then plants her feet firmly, refusing absolutely to take another step forward no matter how insistently anyone tugs at her lead rope.

Jaber commands her sharply to keep moving, yet Amal remains utterly obstinate, straining backward with unexpected, surprising force for such a diminutive animal. She groans loudly and presses her entire body against her mother's flank, almost as if attempting desperately to warn her too. Baffled and growing increasingly frustrated by this bewildering behavior, the herders finally pause and gaze upward toward the rapidly darkening sky. Far off on the horizon, an enormous wall of dark, swirling sand rises rapidly, racing directly toward the exposed and entirely vulnerable caravan.

The herders scramble immediately to locate shelter among the nearby rocky outcrops, huddling together behind a tall, steep dune just as the storm's first violent gusts strike without mercy. The sandstorm thunders past them with overwhelming, relentless force, shaking the very ground beneath their feet, yet everyone survives unharmed within their makeshift shelter, protected fortunately by the dune's considerable height.

For centuries, desert travelers have observed that camels often grow restless, or even stubbornly refuse to move, just before a sandstorm arrives, as though some subtle shift in atmospheric pressure or the ground itself warns them long before any human instrument could ever gauge the coming danger accurately.

After the storm finally subsides and an eerie calm settles once more over the desert, Jaber approaches slowly and pats Amal with unmistakable, genuine respect shining in his weathered eyes. Her peculiar, stubborn instinct had warned the entire caravan of approaching danger long before any human had managed to notice even a single sign of trouble. He realizes, perhaps for the first time in many years, that generations of accumulated Bedouin wisdom have always held that even the youngest animals sometimes sense what human experience alone cannot teach. From that day forward, the herders treat the once-doubted little camel quite differently, feeding her first each morning and relying increasingly on her instincts whenever the weather seems uncertain or potentially threatening. Loyal, perceptive Amal is no longer regarded as the weakest camel in the caravan, but rather as living proof that genuine respect must sometimes be earned through unexpected, admirable moments of courage. She has demonstrated, through one remarkable and frightening afternoon, that even the smallest and youngest member of a group can ultimately prove the bravest of all.

This single remarkable afternoon permanently transformed how an entire caravan viewed its smallest, most doubted member. Loyal, perceptive Amal is no longer regarded as the weakest camel among them, but rather as living proof that genuine respect must sometimes be earned through unexpected, admirable moments of courage, and that true endurance is measured not merely in strength or physical size, but in the quiet, inherited wisdom an animal carries within itself long before anyone around it thinks to notice or appreciate it. Her story travels with the caravan from oasis to oasis, retold by herders who once doubted her, now certain that the smallest companion can prove, in the moment that matters most, the most admirable of all.

keyWords.definition: a big desert animal with a hump that can carry people and goods
keyWords.example: The camel carried heavy bags across the sand.

keyWords.definition: a group of people and animals traveling together, often through a desert
keyWords.example: Our caravan stopped to rest near a well.

keyWords.definition: a dry, sandy place that gets very little rain
keyWords.example: No rain fell on the desert for many months.

keyWords.definition: a person who takes care of and guides animals
keyWords.example: The herder counted the sheep before sunset.

keyWords.definition: a strong wind that blows a lot of sand into the air
keyWords.example: We covered our faces during the sudden sandstorm.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A caravan that gets lost in a sandstorm
A young camel senses a sandstorm and earns respect
A kind herder who teaches young camels tricks
A fast race between two different camel caravans
questions.why: The story tells how Amal, a young camel, senses a sandstorm before the herders and earns their respect by helping keep the caravan safe.

wrong.A: The caravan is not lost; it finds shelter safely.
wrong.C: Jaber does not teach the camels tricks in the story.
wrong.D: There is no race between caravans in the story.

questions.stem: Why does Amal fall behind the other camels at first in the story?
options: She is still small and cannot walk as fast as the big camels
She does not like walking in the desert heat and often stops for shade
She is carrying too many heavy bags on her back this morning
She wants to stay close to the rocks where the grass is green
questions.why: The story says Amal is still small and cannot walk as fast as the big camels, so she falls behind.

wrong.B: The story does not say she dislikes the heat.
wrong.C: The story does not say she carries bags.
wrong.D: There are no rocks mentioned until the storm comes.

questions.stem: Who warns the caravan that a sandstorm is coming, before anyone sees it?
options: An old herder named Jaber
Amal's mother
Amal, the young camel
A bird flying overhead
questions.why: Amal stops and refuses to move before the herders notice the storm, warning them without words.

wrong.A: Jaber does not notice the storm first; he notices it after Amal stops.
wrong.B: Amal's mother does not sense the storm in the story.
wrong.D: No bird is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What happens right after Amal refuses to walk forward?
options: The herders feed her first and let her rest
Amal runs far away from the group alone
The caravan turns back toward home at once
The herders look up and see a sandstorm rising
questions.why: After Amal refuses to move, the herders finally look up at the sky and see the sandstorm rising far away.

wrong.A: The herders feed her first only after the storm, not right after she refuses to walk.
wrong.B: Amal does not run away; she pulls back and groans.
wrong.C: The caravan does not turn back in the story.

questions.stem: Why does Amal refuse to move forward?
options: She is thirsty and wants to find water nearby
She senses danger before anyone else notices
She wants to rest in the shade of a rock
She is angry at her mother for the long walk
questions.why: Amal stops and will not move because she senses something wrong in the air, which turns out to be the coming sandstorm.

wrong.A: The story does not say she is thirsty.
wrong.C: There is no shade mentioned at that moment.
wrong.D: Amal is not angry; she is trying to warn everyone.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Jaber by the end of the story?
options: He now respects Amal and trusts her instincts
He still thinks Amal is too weak to travel
He decides to sell Amal at the next oasis
He leaves the caravan and never returns
questions.why: After the storm, Jaber pats Amal with respect and feeds her first, showing he now trusts and values her.

wrong.B: Jaber's doubts change after Amal senses the storm.
wrong.C: The story never says Jaber sells Amal.
wrong.D: Jaber stays with the caravan after the storm.

questions.stem: In the story, a sandstorm is —
options: a cold rain that falls in the winter
a deep well that is full of clean water
a kind of large animal that lives in the desert
a strong wind that blows a lot of sand into the air
questions.why: The story describes dark sand rising and roaring past the caravan, which is a sandstorm: strong wind carrying sand.

wrong.A: The story says it is sand, not rain.
wrong.B: A sandstorm is not a well.
wrong.C: A sandstorm is weather, not an animal.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that Jaber shakes his head at Amal near the beginning of the story?
options: To show that Jaber is feeling very tired
To explain how caravans are put together
To show that Jaber doubts Amal can finish the trip
To describe exactly what young Amal looks like to everyone
questions.why: Jaber shaking his head shows the reader, early on, that he does not believe Amal has the strength to finish the journey, which makes the ending more surprising.

wrong.A: The head-shaking is about doubt, not tiredness.
wrong.B: The story does not explain how caravans are built.
wrong.D: Shaking his head is not a detailed description of Amal's looks.

LOW.prompt: Do you think the herders were right to feed Amal first after the storm? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think the herders were right to feed Amal first. She sensed the sandstorm before anyone else did, and that warning helped keep the whole caravan safe. Even though Amal was small and slow at the start, she showed that she could be brave and helpful when it mattered most.

keyWords.definition: extremely tired, with very little energy left
keyWords.example: After the long hike, the hikers felt completely exhausted.

keyWords.definition: a feeling or behavior an animal is born with, not something it learns
keyWords.example: Birds fly south in winter by instinct.

keyWords.definition: refusing to change your mind or do what someone else wants
keyWords.example: The stubborn mule would not move from the gate.

keyWords.definition: staying faithful and devoted to someone, even when it is hard
keyWords.example: The loyal dog waited by the door every day.

keyWords.definition: a feeling of admiration for someone because of their qualities or actions
keyWords.example: The new player quickly earned the respect of his teammates.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Amal, a young camel exhausted by the journey, senses a sandstorm through instinct and earns the herders' respect by saving the caravan
A caravan loses its way in the desert and must turn back to the village after a long walk without water or food, and the herders are sad
Jaber teaches young camels how to find hidden wells in the sand, and the herders thank him for his help and give him a gift for it
A camel race decides which caravan reaches the oasis first, and the winners receive a prize from the elders and a place at the well
questions.why: The story follows Amal's struggle to keep up, her instinct-driven warning of the sandstorm, and how that earns her the herders' respect.

wrong.B: The caravan does not lose its way or turn back.
wrong.C: Jaber does not teach the camels to find wells.
wrong.D: There is no race in the story.

questions.stem: Why does Jaber doubt that Amal can finish the journey?
options: He thinks she is afraid of the dark desert nights and will turn back
He believes she dislikes traveling with the other camels in the line
He believes such a small camel lacks the strength for this journey
He thinks she is simply too stubborn to listen to anyone in the group
questions.why: The story says Jaber doubts that such a small, young camel has the strength or endurance to finish such a demanding journey.

wrong.A: The story never mentions fear of the dark.
wrong.B: Nothing suggests Amal dislikes the other camels.
wrong.D: Amal's stubbornness appears later, at the moment of the storm, not as the reason for Jaber's early doubt.

questions.stem: What warns Amal that the sandstorm is coming, according to the story?
options: A loud warning shouted by her friend Jaber
A sudden, unnatural stillness in the air
Thunder rumbling in the distance
A message passed from her mother
questions.why: The story describes the air suddenly growing completely still, which is what alerts Amal before any human notices.

wrong.A: Jaber does not warn anyone; he does not notice the storm yet.
wrong.C: No thunder is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: Amal's mother does not send her a message.

questions.stem: Why does Amal press her body against her mother and refuse to move?
options: She wants to be carried the rest of the way home by her mother
She is too exhausted to stand on her own four legs any more, so she leans on her mother
She is playing a game with her mother in the sand for fun
She is trying, by instinct, to warn her mother that something is wrong
questions.why: The story shows Amal groaning and pushing against her mother as though trying to warn her, driven by instinct, before the storm is seen.

wrong.A: Camels are not carried; the story does not suggest this.
wrong.B: She is not described as too exhausted to stand; she is actively resisting.
wrong.C: This is not described as play; it is urgent, worried behavior.

questions.stem: What does Amal's behavior before the storm suggest about camels?
options: Camels may sense danger through instinct before humans notice any sign of it
Camels cannot sense weather changes at all, so they just follow people.
Camels only react to loud, sudden noises and to nothing else.
Camels are always stubborn for no clear reason, even when they are well.
questions.why: Amal senses the coming sandstorm before any human does, suggesting camels can notice danger through instinct that people miss.

wrong.B: The opposite is shown: Amal clearly senses the coming storm.
wrong.C: There is no loud noise before Amal reacts; the air simply turns still.
wrong.D: Amal's stubbornness in this moment has a clear cause: sensed danger.

questions.stem: Why do the herders begin to treat Amal with more respect after the storm?
options: She is now considered the biggest camel in the whole caravan
She found a hidden well of fresh water near the dunes
She proved to be loyal and perceptive when it mattered most
She finally learned to walk as fast as the grown camels
questions.why: Amal's early warning protected the caravan, showing loyalty and sharp senses, which earns her new respect from the herders.

wrong.A: Amal does not grow bigger in the story.
wrong.B: No well is found in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not say she becomes as fast as the adults.

questions.stem: In the story, the word stubborn describes a camel that —
options: quickly obeys every command it is given
refuses to change what it is doing, even when pushed
falls asleep in the middle of the day
likes to travel much faster than the older camels
questions.why: Amal remains stubborn by refusing to move forward no matter how hard Jaber orders or pulls her.

wrong.A: This is the opposite of stubborn.
wrong.C: Stubborn does not mean sleepy.
wrong.D: Stubborn is about resisting, not speed.

questions.stem: How does Jaber's attitude toward Amal change from the beginning of the story to the end?
options: He dislikes her for the whole long story
He never changes his mind about her, even at the end
He begins respectful and ends doubtful about her skill
He begins doubtful but ends with real respect for her
questions.why: Jaber starts out shaking his head in doubt, but by the end he pats Amal with genuine respect, showing a clear change.

wrong.A: Jaber does not dislike Amal; he doubts her ability, not her character.
wrong.B: His attitude clearly changes after the storm.
wrong.C: This reverses the actual order of events.

MID.prompt: Explain how Amal changed from being doubted to being respected. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Amal changed from being doubted to being respected.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: At the start of the story, Jaber doubts that Amal, a small and exhausted young camel, has the strength to finish the journey. But when the air suddenly turns still, Amal's instinct warns her of danger before any human notices, and she stubbornly refuses to move. Because of her warning, the herders find shelter just before a huge sandstorm strikes. Afterward, Jaber treats Amal with real respect, feeding her first, because she proved to be loyal and perceptive exactly when the caravan needed her most.

keyWords.definition: the ability to keep going through something difficult for a long time
keyWords.example: Marathon runners train for months to build endurance.

keyWords.definition: to depend on someone or something for help or support
keyWords.example: Pilots rely on their instruments when clouds block the view.

keyWords.definition: deserving respect or approval because of good qualities
keyWords.example: Her admirable patience helped calm the frightened child.

keyWords.definition: to judge or measure something, often a level of danger or amount
keyWords.example: The captain tried to gauge how far the storm was from the ship.

keyWords.definition: a member of a traditionally nomadic Arab people of the desert
keyWords.example: The Bedouin family moved their tents to a new grazing area.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: A Bedouin caravan is destroyed by an unavoidable sandstorm, and nobody survives to tell the story of the journey.
Jaber teaches every young camel in the caravan to sense danger, and they all learn it in a single week of training.
A young camel's instinct for danger, dismissed at first, ultimately earns her the caravan's genuine respect and reveals that endurance is not only physical
Camels are naturally better at crossing deserts than humans, which is why the merchants let the camels lead the caravan across the sand without any help.
questions.why: The story centers on Amal's dismissed instinct proving crucial, and on the idea that true endurance includes the quiet wisdom she carries, not just physical strength.

wrong.A: The caravan survives the sandstorm; it is not destroyed.
wrong.B: Jaber does not teach other camels to sense danger.
wrong.D: The story never compares camels and humans in general.

questions.stem: According to the story, why does Jaber doubt Amal at the start of the journey?
options: He questions whether such a small, young camel has the endurance for so demanding a journey
He believes she dislikes traveling alongside the experienced Bedouin herders on long trips
He thinks she is secretly afraid of her own mother and the rest of the herd
He believes she has already injured her leg earlier in the long journey
questions.why: In the story, Jaber doubts a camel so small and young has the strength or endurance to survive such a demanding journey.

wrong.B: The story never says Amal dislikes the herders.
wrong.C: There is no suggestion Amal fears her mother.
wrong.D: No injury is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What specific change in the environment first alerts Amal to the coming sandstorm?
options: A sudden drop in temperature across the dunes
An unnatural stillness in the air
A flash of lightning on the horizon
The sound of distant thunder
questions.why: The story describes the air growing unnaturally still as the desert wind seems to vanish, which is what first alerts Amal.

wrong.A: No temperature drop is described.
wrong.C: The story mentions no lightning.
wrong.D: The story mentions no thunder.

questions.stem: Why do the herders ultimately take shelter behind the dune?
options: Jaber orders a rest stop for the exhausted camels and the herders, who have walked for hours
Amal leads them toward a hidden well in the dunes where there is water and shade for all
The caravan stops at that dune each year to eat, pray, and feed the animals for the night
They notice the wall of sand rising and gauge that a sandstorm is about to strike
questions.why: Once the herders look up and see the wall of sand, they judge, or gauge, that a sandstorm is approaching and rush to shelter.

wrong.A: This is not a planned rest stop; it is an emergency reaction.
wrong.B: There is no well in the story.
wrong.C: The story does not describe this as a yearly stop.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about camels in general from Amal's behavior before the storm?
options: Some camels may rely on instinct to sense approaching danger before humans do
All camels refuse to walk whenever they are tired or thirsty in the desert
Camels are hard for Bedouin herders to train
Camels are mainly useful for carrying heavy loads across the sand
questions.why: Amal senses the storm through instinct well before any human notices a sign, suggesting camels can rely on instinct this way.

wrong.B: Amal's refusal is tied to sensed danger, not ordinary tiredness.
wrong.C: The story shows Bedouin herders successfully guiding camels.
wrong.D: The story's point is about more than carrying loads.

questions.stem: Why does Jaber's view of Amal change so completely by the end of the story?
options: Amal grows larger and stronger than all of the adult camels in the caravan
Amal finds water for the entire caravan in the desert after the storm
Amal's admirable instinct protected the caravan when experience alone could not
Jaber realizes he misjudged most of the young camels he has met
questions.why: Amal's instinct warned the caravan of danger before Jaber's many years of experience could, which is why he comes to admire and respect her.

wrong.A: Amal does not grow larger in the story.
wrong.B: No water is found in the story.
wrong.D: Jaber's change of heart is specific to Amal, not every young camel he has known.

questions.stem: In the story, to gauge something means to —
options: ignore it and think about something else
judge or measure it carefully
celebrate it with a feast
forget about it quickly
questions.why: Jaber glances back to gauge Amal's progress, meaning he judges or measures how she is doing.

wrong.A: Gauging something is paying attention to it, not ignoring it.
wrong.C: Gauge has nothing to do with a feast.
wrong.D: Gauging means carefully judging, not forgetting.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that desert travelers have observed camels' behavior before sandstorms for centuries?
options: To prove that sandstorms occur only once every hundred years in the desert
To suggest that Jaber invented this idea with no real basis
To argue that camels should replace human guides
To show Amal's instinct reflects a real Bedouin tradition, not mere luck
questions.why: This detail connects Amal's individual instinct to a long-recognized pattern, showing her warning was grounded in real desert knowledge rather than coincidence.

wrong.A: This detail is about recognizing warning signs, not how often storms occur.
wrong.B: The idea predates Jaber by centuries of desert travelers' observations.
wrong.C: The story does not argue camels should replace human guides.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says a small or inexperienced member of a group cannot really help the group in a dangerous moment. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that a small or inexperienced member of a group cannot help in a dangerous moment. Amal, the youngest and smallest camel in the caravan, senses the coming sandstorm through instinct long before Jaber, an experienced herder of more than twenty years, notices any sign of it. Her stubborn refusal to move gives the caravan just enough warning to find shelter in time. Someone might argue that experience and strength matter more than instinct, but this story shows that even a young, doubted camel can carry a kind of wisdom that years of experience alone cannot teach, and that endurance is not only about size or strength.

LOW.stem: In the story, what is a caravan?
options: A group of camels and people
A strong wind that blows sand around
A tall rock where herders can hide
A small camel that falls behind a lot
LOW.why: In the text, a caravan is camels and people who cross the desert.

wrong.B: A wind is not a caravan; the storm is separate.
wrong.C: The rocks and dune are places to hide, not the caravan.
wrong.D: Amal is one camel, but a caravan is the whole group.

LOW.stem: Where did the herders hide from the storm?
options: Inside a deep cave
Under their tents
Next to a big dune
In a cool river
LOW.why: In the story, the herders look for a safe place to hide from the storm.

wrong.A: No cave is in the story.
wrong.B: The herders did not use tents.
wrong.D: There is no river in the story.

LOW.stem: Why do the herders feed Amal first after the storm?
options: She walked the fastest in the caravan.
She was the oldest camel in the group.
She carried more than all the others.
She sensed the danger before they did.
LOW.why: Amal felt the storm first, so the herders now feed her first.

wrong.A: Amal is not fast; she falls behind.
wrong.B: Amal is a young camel.
wrong.C: Amal is small and is not said to carry the most.

LOW.stem: What happened right after the storm went past the herders?
options: The air went still.
Jaber patted Amal.
The herders ran to the rocks.
Amal fell behind again.
LOW.why: After the storm, Jaber pats Amal.

wrong.A: The air went still before the storm.
wrong.C: The herders ran to the rocks before the storm passed.
wrong.D: Amal falling behind happened earlier, before the storm.

MID.stem: In the story, what does the word "instinct" mean?
options: A heavy load that a camel must carry
A natural sense that warns an animal
A tall dune that gives shelter
A rope the herders use to lead camels
MID.why: An old instinct tells Amal danger is near before her eyes can see it, so it is a natural sense.

wrong.A: The camels carry supplies, but that is not an instinct.
wrong.C: A dune is a place for shelter.
wrong.D: A rope is not something that warns Amal.

MID.stem: What did Amal do after she sniffed the air again and again?
options: She ran far ahead of the caravan.
She lay down to rest in the sand.
She refused to take another step.
She pulled the others forward.
MID.why: In the story, she sniffed the air and then would not move.

wrong.A: Amal stopped moving instead of running ahead.
wrong.B: She stayed standing and stubborn, not resting.
wrong.D: She held back, not pulled others forward.

MID.stem: Why did the herders stop and look up at the sky?
options: They heard thunder in the clouds.
Jaber saw a bird flying overhead.
They wanted to rest in the shade.
Amal's odd actions confused them.
MID.why: Amal groaned and pressed against her mother, so the confused herders looked up.

wrong.A: The text mentions no thunder.
wrong.B: No bird is mentioned.
wrong.C: They did not stop to rest; they stopped because of Amal.

MID.stem: Why does the author call Amal "the once-doubted little camel"?
options: Jaber used to doubt she could finish
She had once been lost in the desert
She used to be a much bigger camel
The herders had once forgotten her
MID.why: Jaber at first doubted that small Amal had the strength to finish the trip.

wrong.B: Amal is not said to have been lost.
wrong.C: Amal is still small.
wrong.D: The herders doubted her; they did not forget her.

HIGH.stem: In the story, what does the word "endurance" mean?
options: The speed needed to win a short race
The weight that a camel can lift
The strength to keep going for hours
The talent for finding water in sand
HIGH.why: Amal falls behind and gets tired, and Jaber doubts she has enough endurance to survive, so it means lasting strength.

wrong.A: The trip is long, not a short race.
wrong.B: The problem is tiredness, not lifting weight.
wrong.D: Finding water is never mentioned.

HIGH.stem: How long had Jaber guided caravans across the desert?
options: More than twenty years
Only a few short months
Just since Amal was born
About five years
HIGH.why: The text says he has guided caravans for more than two decades.

wrong.B: Jaber has long experience.
wrong.C: The text does not tie his work to Amal's birth.
wrong.D: Two decades means about twenty years, not five.

HIGH.stem: Why do the herders rely on Amal's instincts when the weather feels uncertain?
options: She has become the strongest camel in the group.
Her instinct warned them before they saw a sign.
She knows the shortest way to the oasis.
Jaber is too tired to watch the sky himself.
HIGH.why: Her instinct warned the caravan of the storm long before any human noticed.

wrong.A: Amal is still described as small and young.
wrong.C: The oasis route is not tied to her instincts.
wrong.D: The text does not say Jaber is too tired to look.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author show the wall of dark sand only after describing Amal's strange behavior?
options: To prove the herders were not brave
To show the storm was weaker than feared
To explain how camels cross the desert
To build suspense before the danger appears
HIGH.why: Amal's warning signs come first, so readers wonder what is wrong before the storm is revealed.

wrong.A: The herders ran for shelter; the text does not say they were not brave.
wrong.B: The storm is powerful and thunders past with great force.
wrong.C: The passage is about the storm, not how camels cross the desert.
